title: Oswald et al. (2010) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False. Distinguish the young-old group (ages 65–79) from the old-old group (ages 80–94), and check sample denominators, measurement methods, and analysis stages. These cross-sectional associations do not establish individual development or causal effects.

items.prompt: Young-old participants were more often widowed than old-old participants, whereas old-old participants were more often married.
items.explanation: The pattern was the reverse: young-old participants were more often married, and old-old participants were more often widowed.

items.prompt: In the final descriptive sample, women represented 49.1% of the young-old group and 57.4% of the old-old group.
items.explanation: After excluding 21 participants because of missing data, the sample included 226 young-old participants, 49.1% women, and 155 old-old participants, 57.4% women.

items.prompt: The researchers measured environmental indicators through a questionnaire without conducting objective environmental assessments in participants' homes or neighborhoods.
items.explanation: Room counts and floor area were reported by participants, as were perceived accessibility and comfort. Even the indicators the authors labeled objective were collected through the questionnaire, rather than an observer's home assessment.

items.prompt: Perceived housing accessibility summed three items covering amenities inside the home, the front door, and neighborhood public transport access.
items.explanation: The accessibility score summed two items: barrier-free access to amenities within the home and access to the front door without stairs. Public transport access was not a third item in this score.

items.prompt: ADL and IADL each assessed seven activities, and both scales ranged from 0 to 14.
items.explanation: Each activity was scored 2 for functioning without help, 1 for functioning with some help, and 0 when it was no longer possible. Higher total scores indicated greater independence.

items.prompt: Differences between age groups in both means and frequencies were tested only with zero-order Pearson correlations.
items.explanation: Mean differences were examined with analysis of variance and frequency differences with chi-square tests. Zero-order Pearson correlations addressed relationships among variables in a separate analysis stage.

items.prompt: Old-old participants had larger homes on average and reported about one more of the ten comfort-related amenities than young-old participants.
items.explanation: The young-old group, not the old-old group, had larger homes on average and reported about one additional comfort-related amenity.

items.prompt: Life satisfaction represented the cognitive dimension of well-being and was assessed with one self-rating item from 0 to 10.
items.explanation: The 11-point response scale ranged from 0, totally unsatisfied, to 10, totally satisfied. It measured an evaluation of life satisfaction, not cognitive functioning.

items.prompt: In the zero-order correlations, neighborhood quality and outdoor place attachment were more strongly related to life satisfaction in the young-old group.
items.explanation: Both neighborhood indicators had stronger correlations with life satisfaction in the old-old group. These are cross-sectional associations, not evidence that their effects grew as the same individuals aged.

items.prompt: The study found no significant age-group differences in basic housing accessibility, neighborhood evaluations, perceived social neighborhood quality, or available social partners in the area.
items.explanation: Differences were reported for living space, comfort, living with a partner, and functional capacity, but not for the listed accessibility and neighborhood indicators. A nonsignificant difference does not establish that the groups are exactly identical.

items.prompt: In the zero-order correlations, housing comfort was positively related to both life satisfaction and functional capacity only in the young-old group.
items.explanation: The authors report this positive pattern for young-old participants, but not for old-old participants. This statement concerns the zero-order correlations rather than an independent effect established in the regression models.

items.prompt: The authors concluded that societal housing policy should focus exclusively on barrier-free building standards.
items.explanation: They proposed expanding the focus beyond objective building standards to include perceived aspects of housing and the neighborhood in a broader approach to planning.

items.prompt: The follow-up interaction tests supported age-group differences only for apartment size, not for neighborhood quality or outdoor place attachment.
items.explanation: The follow-up analyses provided evidence of reliable age-group differences in the explanatory value of all three indicators: apartment size, neighborhood quality, and outdoor place attachment. These tests concern differences in associations across groups, not developmental changes within individuals.

items.prompt: The young-old and old-old groups had comparable average durations of residence in the same place.
items.explanation: The discussion explicitly notes that mean durations of residence in the same place were comparable across the two age groups.

items.prompt: The authors caution that cross-sectional age differences should not be mistaken for individual developmental change and that change over time requires longitudinal data.
items.explanation: These data cannot establish the causal direction of environmental associations or show whether their influence increases or decreases as individuals move from young-old to old-old age.
